headline: The latest HRRR moved its lone downpour from 10 PM tonight to about 4 to 6 AM Friday and made it stronger (0.54 in in 3 hours, nearly all in one hour), but no other model backs it, so the consensus stays at 0.39 in, below Yellow.

summary.text: HRRR's single strong cell moved from 10 PM tonight to about 4–6 AM Friday and grew from 0.34 in to 0.54 in (0.48 in in one hour). Consensus unchanged at 0.39 in.
Wettest 3 hours in the next 72 h: HRRR 0.54 in, GFS 0.54 (copies HRRR), RRFS 0.39, NBM 0.23, ECMWF 0.07. Consensus (HRRR ×1.25 = 0.68, RRFS 0.39, NBM 0.23: middle value) 0.39 in.
Most likely no more than water on the sidewalk in a downpour. Yellow (garage) needs about 0.71 in in 3 hours or a measured 0.40 in hour; only the HRRR cell comes close.
Scattered showers this afternoon and evening. HRRR's cell around 4–6 AM Friday; RRFS and NBM favor steadier showers about 7–10 AM Friday. A light round Saturday evening.
Friday's 7.9 ft high at 8:32 AM runs about 9.9 ft on the NOAA Bay model (~2 ft surge), right with the Friday-morning showers. Caltrain channel 0.76 ft, rising slowly, far below Monitoring (2.8 ft).
Clear drain grates this afternoon. No cars need to move on the consensus; check the page around 4–9 AM Friday, and move cars if a 0.40 in hour shows up.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: The upper low is moving south and inland. NWS San Francisco's 10:30 AM update says showers continue across the region through early Friday afternoon, with a slight chance of thunderstorms near the coast into early afternoon before the instability shifts inland and the thunder threat fades for the Bay Area. A colder front late tonight into Friday gradually cuts back the showers, followed by cold mornings Friday and Saturday. A weaker system late Saturday favors the North Bay, and NWS flags Tuesday into Wednesday of next week as the next chance for heavier rain (mainly North Bay) along with more coastal flooding from the approaching king tides.

sections.title: What changed and model trends
sections.text:
Since the 10:20 AM discussion, the new HRRR (11 AM run) dropped its 10 PM cell and instead puts a strong one early Friday: 0.48 in in the hour ending 5 AM and 0.06 in the next hour, for 0.54 in in its wettest 3 hours (up from 0.34 in). Its 15-minute output is less concentrated, with about 0.22 in from 4:30 to 5:00 AM and light rain after. GFS shows the same 0.48 in hour because it uses HRRR in the short range, so it is not an independent vote.

The other models do not support a burst that strong. RRFS (4 AM run) has 0.39 in in its wettest 3 hours, about 7 to 10 AM Friday, with no hour above 0.15 in. NBM has 0.23 in over the same 7 to 10 AM window, no hour above 0.08 in. ECMWF is nearly dry here, 0.07 in at most in 3 hours. Like this morning's 10 PM cell, I treat the HRRR's 5 AM hour as a possible shower or thunderstorm cell with low confidence, not a trend. What the models do agree on is a wetter few hours Friday morning, between roughly 4 and 10 AM.

The dashboard's consensus (HRRR ×1.25 = 0.68, RRFS 0.39, NBM 0.23; middle value) is 0.39 in, the same as at 10 AM. That seems reasonable for a showery pattern. The way it ends up worse is if the HRRR cell, or one like it, actually happens: at its ×1.25 bias it would be 0.68 in, just under the 0.71 in Yellow line, and a measured 0.40 in hour would trip Yellow by itself.

Storm totals for the next 72 hours stay light: RRFS 0.82 in, GFS 0.71, NBM 0.64, HRRR 0.54 (its run ends Saturday morning), ECMWF 0.34.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text:
The Bay continues to run about 2 ft above the predicted tide on NOAA's Bay model. Tonight's 6.2 ft high at 8:09 PM shows about 8.3 ft on the model. The low at 2:07 AM Friday (1.6 ft predicted) stays near 3.4 ft. The tide is then rising fast during the HRRR's cell, from about 5.9 ft at 5 AM to 8.7 ft at 7 AM on the model, and Friday's 7.9 ft high at 8:32 AM peaks near 9.9 ft, right on top of the RRFS and NBM shower window. Saturday's high is higher still, 8.4 ft predicted at 9:06 AM (the Bay model run ends before then).

NWS extended the Coastal Flood Advisory for the Bay shoreline until 11 AM Saturday, with up to 1.8 ft of surge, and says the Bays may be upgraded to a Coastal Flood Warning as the king tides approach. High water in the Bay slows how fast the channel can drain on Friday and Saturday mornings.

Channel: the gauge upstream of Caltrain fell to 0.24 ft at 10:46 AM, then rose with the midday showers to 0.76 ft at 12:58 PM, far below county Flood Monitoring (2.8 ft). At Alameda de las Pulgas it is 0.37 ft at 1 PM (Monitoring 3.18 ft).

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Light showers. The Caltrain rain gauge recorded 0.04 in in the 11 AM hour and 0.04 in so far in the 1 PM hour (last reading 1:06 PM), 0.08 in over the last 3 hours. Its 24-hour total is now 0.68 in, since Wednesday's heavy hours have dropped out of that window. Both channel gauges are low; the Caltrain one is creeping up with the showers.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: Low for a long soaking rain, moderate for a single strong cell. The models agree only light to moderate showers are left, but they keep moving the strongest cell around: the HRRR had it at 10 PM tonight in its 8 AM run and at 5 AM Friday in its 11 AM run, and no other model has anything like it. That kind of jumping is typical of shower cells the model cannot pin down. A thunderstorm over a few blocks can still beat every model, and the ground is wet. Friday morning stacks the odds a little: the wettest model hours, a high tide with about 2 ft of surge, and darkness. Most likely outcome: no street flooding, possibly water on the sidewalk in a downpour.

sections.title: What to do
sections.text:
• This afternoon, while it is light, clear leaves and debris from the street drain grates and yard drains.
• No need to move cars out of the cul-de-sac on the consensus. If you'd rather not be caught by an early-morning cell, moving cars before bed is a cheap precaution.
• Check the dashboard around 4 to 9 AM Friday; if the 1-hour burst alarm trips (0.40 in in one hour), move cars and watch the street.
• Take timestamped photos if water reaches the sidewalk or yards.
• Expect cold mornings Friday and Saturday.
• Don't drive or walk through moving water.
